title: Module 4 · Lesson 1 — How LLM inference actually consumes a GPU

lines: Welcome to lesson one: how LLM inference actually consumes a GPU.
Every scaling answer in this domain starts here.
Picture a lawyer pasting a sixty-page contract into an assistant, asking for the risky clauses.
The screen sits blank for eight seconds, then the answer streams out smoothly.
That pause and that stream are two phases with different bottlenecks.
Prefill reads the whole prompt in parallel, saturating the GPU's compute.

say.1: Pree-fill reads the whole prompt in parallel, saturating the GPU's compute.

lines: Prefill sets the time to first token, and its cost grows with prompt length.
So a long contract, or a long agent transcript, means a long wait.

say.0: Pree-fill sets the time to first token, and its cost grows with prompt length.

lines: Decode then writes one token at a time, limited by memory bandwidth.
It sets the gap between tokens, while GPU compute sits mostly idle.
Because the phases stress different resources, NVIDIA Dynamo runs them on separate GPU pools.
Each pool is sized on its own, and the KV cache is passed between them.

say.1: Each pool is sized on its own, and the kay-vee cache is passed between them.

lines: Now fifty lawyers log in, and the GPU runs out of memory, though the weights fit.
The culprit is the KV cache, which stores keys and values for every token already processed.

say.1: The culprit is the kay-vee cache, which stores keys and values for every token already processed.

lines: It grows with batch size, sequence length, layers, and hidden size.
So the cache, not the weights, limits how many requests fit.
Agents hurt here, because a forty-step run is one very long sequence.
The fixes are paged attention, FP8 cache quantization, prefix caching, and compaction.
Static batching waits for a full batch, then stalls on the longest sequence.
Continuous batching hands each finished slot to a queued request, for a multi-fold throughput gain.
Batch size is the dial between throughput and latency.
Bigger batches raise total tokens per second, but slow each request.
NIM gives you continuous batching, prefix caching, and quantization out of the box.
But quantization is never free, so re-run your own evaluation first.

say.0: Nim gives you continuous batching, prefix caching, and quantization out of the box.

lines: Self-host NIM for data residency or steady volume; use a hosted API for spiky traffic.
Both are OpenAI-compatible, so switching is usually a base URL change.

say.0: Self-host nim for data residency or steady volume; use a hosted API for spiky traffic.

lines: On the exam, to hit a strict latency target, cap the batch size and add replicas.
Now read on for the details.
